In [[probability theory]], a '''subordinator''' is a [[stochastic process]] that is [[non-negative]] and whose increments are [[stationary increments|stationary]] and [[independent increments|independent]].<ref name="KallebergFoundations290" /> Subordinators are a special class of [[Lévy process]] that play an important role in the theory of [[local time (mathematics)|local time]].<ref name="KallenbergMeasures651" /> In this context, subordinators describe the evolution of time within another stochastic process, the subordinated stochastic process. In other words, a subordinator will determine the [[random variable|random]] number of "time steps" that occur within the subordinated process for a given unit of chronological time.

In order to be a subordinator a process must be a [[Lévy process]]<ref name=applebaum>{{cite web|title=Lectures on Lévy processes and Stochastic calculus, Braunschweig; Lecture 2: Lévy processes|url=http://www.applebaum.staff.shef.ac.uk/Brauns2notes.pdf|author=Applebaum, D.|pages=37–53|publisher=University of Sheffield}}</ref>. It also must be increasing, [[almost surely]],<ref name=applebaum/> or an [[additive process]].<ref name=Li>{{cite journal |last1=Li |first1=Jing |last2=Li |first2=Lingfei |last3=Zhang |first3=Gongqiu |title=Pure jump models for pricing and hedging VIX derivatives |journal=Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control |year=2017 |volume=74 |doi=10.1016/j.jedc.2016.11.001}}</ref>

== Definition ==
A subordinator is a [[real-valued stochastic process]] <math> X=(X_t)_{t \geq 0} </math> that is a [[non-negative]] and a [[Lévy process]].<ref name="KallebergFoundations290" />
Subordinators are the stochastic processes <math> X=(X_t)_{t \geq 0} </math> that have all of the following properties: 
* <math> X_0=0 </math> [[almost surely]]
* <math> X </math> is non-negative, meaning <math> X_t  \geq 0 </math> for all <math> t </math>
* <math> X </math>  has [[stationary increments]], meaning that for <math> t \geq 0 </math> and <math> h > 0 </math>, the distribution of the random variable <math> Y_{t,h}:=X_{t+h} - X_t </math>  depends only on <math> h</math>  and not on <math> t </math>
* <math> X </math> has [[independent increments]], meaning that for all <math> n </math> and all <math> t_0 < t_1 < \dots < t_n </math> , the random variables <math> (Y_i)_{i=0, \dots, n-1} </math> defined by <math> Y_i=X_{t_{i+1}}-X_{t_{i}} </math> are [[Independence (probability theory)|independent]] of each other
* The paths of <math> X </math> are [[càdlàg]], meaning they are continuous from the right everywhere and the limits from the left exist everywhere

==Examples==
The [[variance gamma process]] can be described as a [[Brownian motion]] subject to a [[gamma process|gamma subordinator]].<ref name=applebaum/>  If a [[Wiener process|Brownian motion]], <math>W(t)</math>, with drift <math>\theta t</math> is subjected to a random time change which follows a [[gamma process]], <math>\Gamma(t; 1, \nu)</math>, the variance gamma process will follow:

: <math>
 X^{VG}(t; \sigma, \nu, \theta) \;:=\; \theta \,\Gamma(t; 1, \nu) + \sigma\,W(\Gamma(t; 1, \nu)).
</math>

The [[Cauchy process]] can be described as a [[Brownian motion]] subject to a [[Lévy distribution|Lévy subordinator]].<ref name=applebaum/>

== Representation ==
Every subordinator <math> X=(X_t)_{t \geq 0} </math> can be written as
:<math> X_t = at + \int_0^t  \int_0^\infty x  \; \Theta(  \mathrm ds \; \mathrm  dx )</math>
where
* <math> a \geq 0 </math> is a scalar and
* <math> \Theta </math> is a [[Poisson process]] on  <math> (0, \infty)  \times (0, \infty) </math> with [[intensity measure]] <math> \operatorname E \Theta = \lambda \otimes \mu </math>. Here <math> \mu </math> is a [[measure (mathematics)|measure]] on <math> (0, \infty ) </math> with <math> \int_0^\infty \max(x,1) \; \mu (\mathrm dx) < \infty </math>, and <math> \lambda </math> is the [[Lebesgue measure]].

The measure <math> \mu </math> is called the [[Lévy measure]] of the subordinator, and the pair <math> (a, \mu) </math> is called the characteristics of the subordinator.

Conversely, any scalar <math> a \geq 0 </math> and measure <math> \mu </math> on <math> (0, \infty) </math> with <math> \int \max(x,1) \; \mu (\mathrm dx) < \infty </math> define a subordinator with characteristics <math> (a, \mu) </math> by the above relation.<ref name="KallebergFoundations287" /><ref name="KallebergFoundations290" />
